text: Ask HN: Where do you see Software in 5 years? | Hacker News Hacker News new | past | comments | ask | show | jobs | submit login Ask HN: Where do you see Software in 5 years? 5 points by Odbyteusz 1 hour ago | hide | past | favorite | 6 comments I wanted to hear some good opinions on all things AI and how they transform the Software industry. I'm anxious about the future and lack the foresight to form any opinion on what to do next. For context, I'm a L4 SWE that has more or less say 5-10 yrs of exp. I've enjoyed my work throughout my career, AI makes me ship more, much more than I could do 3 years ago. I feel I use it well and it translates into really good software. That said, what do you think happens in years to come with the Software industry in general? Do you think we'll go through a massive erosion of jobs? What's your perspective on that? I'm asking because I honestly don't know what to do: I can try to always keep up to date with newest technologies, best practices, but I'm only me; if the demand for SWEs and jobs falls to the floor, I'm not sure I'll always get a place at the table (i.e. land a job) and I'm wondering whether I should try to do something else in some other industry. It feels weird to be in a good position in life and still constantly worry about it getting worse. austin-cheney 1 hour ago | next [–] In 5 years time software will exist in 3 silos. It's really not any different today, except the talent will continue to diverge. Silo 1 - This will be employers strongly forcing AI for most task completion. This will be most large corporate employers and most start ups. There will be little to no working knowledge of the internals of large applications and these employers will bleed money on outside consultants to occasionally provide manual maintenance and security hot fixes. Everything will continue to look good from the outside, but really its a messy house of cards. Silo 2 - This will be institutional shops of skilled experts. Game companies that own internally developed rendering engines, kernel developers, independent open source, and systems architects come to mind. These will be people that might occasionally dabble in AI for various things, but they manually modify their code. These are experts who do not gain productivity by offloading their greatest challenges to AI. Silo 3 - The consulting class. This is where the money will be. Technology design firms already do most of this, but the problems these consultants solve for their clients will be greater and the clients will be less capable. These people will explode in demand, but supply will likely remain unchanged, because experts are hard to grow and the corporate world won't produce them. --- I also predict the job recruitment industry will struggle as demand for talent stratifies, because software as an industry struggles to identify talent. This problem will remain unsolved until something catastrophic happens and most employers need to simultaneously unload liability in ways they are currently forced to accept it internally. Fear of bankruptcy, loss of money, and complete destruction of business are not strong enough motivators to move the needle on this. reply mariusziskra 0 minutes ago | parent | next [–] I partially agree with these silos; there's one more aspect to consider. The largest players, like OpenAI and Antropic, are creating an increasingly large ecosystem, absorbing more and more tools that could be standalone entities. So, by purchasing access to a single platform, we'll get everything we need. If they don't have something and there's a market for it, they'll create it in a matter of days. On the other hand, I see a trend of bypassing standard user interfaces. We have chats, voice communication is being developed, so in the future (if we still have it), we'll only need a few applications to work. reply spottedmarley 31 minutes ago | prev | next [–] In 5 years I don't see myself using any software that I didn't design and build myself.
